claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is primarily controlled by the extent of Al-induced short-range chemical ordering.
A moderate degree of short-range ordering stabilizes a coherent intermetallic or BCC-like phase.
The moderately ordered phase enables high-temperature strength.
The moderately ordered phase enables radiation tolerance.
The moderately ordered phase enables environmental resistance.
Avoiding excessive ordering preserves cryogenic toughness by preventing excessive brittleness.
The proposed as-cast, near-equiatomic starting alloy is primarily disordered.
The proposed starting alloy has a mixed FCC/BCC microstructure.
Systematic variation of Al concentration and annealing is intended to produce different levels of short-range chemical order.
Al clustering constitutes the proposed short-range-order structural mediator.
The degree of Al clustering modulates formation and stability of the intermetallic or BCC-like phase.
Increasing Al content and applying ordering-promoting heat treatments alter local bonding and electronic structure.
The changes in local bonding and electronic structure encourage transformation from a disordered state to a moderately ordered phase.
Ordering enhances high-temperature strength by stabilizing the phase.
Ordering enhances radiation tolerance by stabilizing the phase.
Excessive ordering causes brittleness at cryogenic temperatures.
A fully disordered state provides insufficient high-temperature performance.
An intermediate ordering level will improve high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, and radiation tolerance relative to the baseline disordered state.
An intermediate ordering level will retain adequate cryogenic toughness.
Mixed-phase baseline alloys typically provide less optimized combinations of mechanical properties.
